newsitem.title: BOSNIA: Persecution of Serbs in Sarajevo suburbs resumes.
newsitem.headline: Persecution of Serbs in Sarajevo suburbs resumes.

text.p: Serbs still living in Sarajevo after their territory was transferred to Bosnian Federation rule were being harassed anew with beatings, arson and draft summonses, U.N. monitors said on Tuesday.

Alex Ivanko, spokesman for the International Police Task Force (IPTF) in postwar Bosnia, said repeated intervention by international peace officials curbed anti-Serb activities last summer, but it had resurged in the past two weeks.

More than 50,000 Serbs fled the suburbs last winter during their post-war transfer to Moslem-dominated authority under the Dayton peace treaty. But 8,000 stayed on assurances they would not face reprisals for a separatist Serb siege of the capital.
"We have worrying reports from our civil affairs officers in Sarajevo of renewed violations of the human rights of Serbs in the suburbs," Ivanko told a news conference.

International human rights monitors said many incidents in the past two weeks targeted members of the Serb Sarajevo Democratic Initiative, an interest group formed by Serbs who did not join the wintertime exodus.
The house of a prominent Serb lawyer was firebombed and arsonists also attacked a home belonging to a Serb who was mayor of suburban Sarajevo before the handover but did not flee.

Human-rights monitors said the 62-year-old stepmother of the ex-mayor was severely beaten with iron bars by thugs who broke into her home. Another elderly Serb woman was assaulted and a Serb family was evicted from their home.
Attempts to eject Serb families from their homes without legal basis were a constant problem, one monitor told Reuters.
Another Serb woman said Moslem neighbours had poisoned her dog and vandalised her home.
Ivanko also cited a series of notices sent to Serb men aged 16 to 60 in the suburb of Ilidza to register for the draft.
Ivanko said the summonses "smacked of harassment" since armed forces in the Moslem and Croat parts of the Federation had been largely demobilised in keeping with the Dayton treaty.

Attacks on minority Serbs have been typically the handiwork of local Moslem gangs or Moslem refugees avenging their wartime expulsion from the suburbs or from Serb-held eastern Bosnia, which was plagued by massacres and other atrocities.
Moslem police officers in the suburbs have often failed to prevent violence against Serbs or have even taken part in it.
Virtually no one has been prosecuted after hundreds of attacks that have occurred mainly in the dead of night, when a curfew should theoretically keep everyone off the streets.
Bosnian Moslem leaders insist lawlessness in the suburbs is nothing compard to the systematic persecution of Moslems on Serb-held territory during the 1992-95 war.

But international authorities say the Federation, an amalgam of Moslem and Croat-ruled lands, cannot afford to tolerate human-rights abuses if it wants to preserve the favour of would-be Western benefactors needed for reconstruction.
"We believe the situation is deteriorating once again and as previously we will apply political pressure (to stop the violence). We hope this approach will work again," said Ivanko.
"We hope federation authorities and police will do their utmost to ensure that the human rights of all citizens of Sarajevo are respected."
